column6: Joseph says God sent him ahead to preserve a remnant and keep his family alive; this is the Hebrew Joseph scene behind the commentary's Qur'anic notice of Joseph's being preferred, joined here to baqiyya.

A forgotten sheaf must be left for the alien, orphan, and widow, so that God blesses the owner. It reverses the commentary's negative “forgotten residue” by making an overlooked remainder provision for vulnerable people.

column5: fallen grapes left for poor and alien
column6: Israel may not strip the vineyard or gather its fallen grapes, but must leave them for poor people and resident aliens; discarded produce becomes deliberate generosity.
Boaz orders workers to pull grain from bundles and leave it for Ruth to glean without rebuke, a narrative instance of turning surplus and leftovers toward a migrant widow's need.
Judah's surviving remnant will take root below and bear fruit above, merging the commentary's positive remnant with its pasture-and-lasting-fruit imagery.
Heavens vanish, earth wears out, and inhabitants die, while God's salvation is forever and righteousness is not shattered; it makes the temporal/enduring comparison cosmic.
A human comes forth like a flower and withers, fleeing like a shadow that does not remain, a close poetic companion to the commentary's flower and non-abiding world.
Treasures of wickedness do not profit, whereas righteousness delivers from death; the proverb makes source and moral quality decisive for what counts as beneficial wealth.
Riches do not profit on the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death, pressing the commentary's contrast between present possession and ultimate outcome.
When one fixes one's eyes on wealth, it is gone and flies heavenward like an eagle; it is a concrete warning against treating visible wealth as what remains.
Jeshurun grows fat, abandons the God who made him, and despises the Rock of salvation; it gives worldly abundance the same spiritual danger as the commentary's preference for dunya.

column5: what accompanies a person at death
column6: The teaching says silver, gold, and precious stones do not accompany a person at death, while Torah and good deeds do; it sharply distinguishes temporary possession from what remains.

column5: today for doing, tomorrow for reward
column6: The talmudic reading of the commandment says this day is for performing them and the next for receiving reward, making present moral action and future recompense distinct without making present life the final good.
God alone possesses immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, closely corresponding to the commentary's statement that enduring being belongs uniquely to God.
The coming judge gathers wheat into the barn and burns chaff with unquenchable fire, combining selected produce, discarded plant matter, and lasting adverse judgment.

column5: good fish collected, bad thrown out
column6: In the net parable, fish are sorted: the good are collected into containers and the bad thrown outside. It is a precise sorting image for selected good and rejected refuse.
Jesus explains the net as a final separation of the evil from the righteous, giving the preceding culling image an explicitly eschatological value judgment.

column5: the least identified with the king
column6: Care given to the least of the king's brothers is counted as care given to the king himself, reversing any association of socially low people with discardable material.

column5: God and wealth as rival masters
column6: No one can serve God and wealth because divided service produces love for one and contempt for the other; this is an explicit account of preference as allegiance.
Jesus tells the rich man to give his possessions to the poor and have treasure in heaven, turning a costly redistribution into an enduring treasure.
Those who persevere in good work and seek glory, honor, and incorruptibility receive eternal life, articulating a pursuit of lasting good through action.
Paul reads Israel's survival through the Elijah narrative as a remnant according to gracious election, giving a Christian interpretation of the morally preserved remainder.
When the earthly tent is destroyed, believers have an eternal, God-made house in heaven; the image makes earthly dissolution and lasting dwelling a direct pair.
The generous person scatters gifts to the poor and his righteousness remains forever, directly uniting self-giving with the commentary's positive language of what remains.
Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; the agricultural metaphor turns the commentary's two-sided choice into two opposed harvests.
Those whose minds are set on earthly things have destruction as their end, with appetite as god and shame as glory; it supplies a concrete New Testament diagnosis of worldly preference.
Believers' citizenship is in heaven and they await a savior from there, providing the positive location corresponding to the rejection of merely earthly-mindedness.
Those raised with Christ are instructed to seek the things above, where Christ is, making selection of an upper and lasting good an explicit practice.
The command to set the mind on things above rather than things on earth is a concise counterpart to refusing to privilege dunya.
Land that produces a useful crop for those who cultivate it receives blessing from God, setting fruitful vegetation on the accepted side of a moral agricultural image.
Land producing thorns and thistles is rejected, near a curse, and ends in burning; it supplies a fully developed counterpart to pasture becoming useless refuse.
God is not unjust so as to forget the work and love shown in serving the saints, turning 87:6's not-forgetting into the preservation of acts of care.
What can be shaken is removed so that what cannot be shaken may remain, a close conceptual formulation of sifting away what does not endure.
The person who continues in the perfect law is not a forgetful hearer but an active doer and is blessed, a specific ethical contrast for the commentary's forgetting motif.
A branch that does not remain in Christ is thrown outside, withers, and is gathered for fire; it joins abiding, vegetable waste, and adverse finality.
Builders use either gold, silver, and precious stones or wood, hay, and straw, a material hierarchy that gives the commentary's selected-versus-dross image a concrete test case.
The day exposes each person's work and fire tests its quality, so apparent building material is sorted by what endures testing.

column5: self-styled rich who are truly poor
column6: The wealthy self-assessment is exposed as wretched, poor, blind, and naked; it overturns worldly measures of value in the commentary's register of high and low.
Those who die in the Lord rest from labor and their deeds follow them, specifying a form of good that survives the end of earthly life.

column5: sharing perishable goods because of imperishable goods
column6: The Two Ways instruction requires sharing with a needy brother and argues that participants in imperishable things should share perishable things all the more; it unites other-preference with a hierarchy of goods.
At death dust returns to earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it; it offers a restrained biblical account of bodily transience beside a Godward remainder.
Wealth gained hastily dwindles, while gradual gathering increases it, adding a concrete temporal test to the commentary's concern for rightly qualified wealth.
The person who gets riches unjustly leaves them in midlife and ends as a fool, combining unclean source with wealth's failure to remain.

column5: giving to poor as loan to God
column6: The one gracious to the poor lends to the LORD, who repays the deed; it makes voluntary preference for a needy other an act with divine return.
Tobit's father says almsgiving lays up a good treasure for the day of need, a Jewish exhortation to turn possessions into a durable good through giving.

column5: possessions and worry / Torah and life to come
column6: Hillel contrasts increased possessions and worry with acquiring Torah and life in the world to come, giving an interpretive hierarchy for worldly accumulation.
God clothes field grass that exists today and is put into an oven tomorrow; the image closely accompanies the commentary's grass, flower, and rapidly discarded vegetation.
